kurz: Most money is created as a book entry at a commercial bank when it grants a loan, and not in the printing press.

bloecke.md:
A bank grants a loan of €300,000. The transaction can be shown in two lines of bookkeeping. On the assets side, a claim on the borrower is created; on the liabilities side, a sight deposit of the same amount is created and credited to her current account. No other account is debited, and no saver loses anything. The bank's balance sheet is then €300,000 larger than before, and the economy's money supply has grown by the same amount.

This contradicts the widespread idea that a bank collects savings deposits and passes them on as loans. The Deutsche Bundesbank explicitly rejected this idea in its Monthly Report of April 2017. The report states that a bank can grant loans

bloecke.text: without any prior inflows of customer deposits
bloecke.quelle: Deutsche Bundesbank, Monthly Report April 2017 (English edition)

bloecke.md: The deposit is therefore the result of lending and not its precondition. The process also works in reverse. If the borrower repays €1,000, the claim on the assets side falls by this amount, and €1,000 of book money disappears on the liabilities side. The money used for the repayment thereby ceases to exist. An economy's money supply therefore only grows as long as more new loans are granted than are repaid.

bloecke.md:
## Two separate money circuits

Two different kinds of money circulate side by side in the monetary system. [[Central bank money]] consists of cash and the balances that banks hold at their central bank. It is a claim on the central bank. Only banks have access to it, along with everyone who holds cash in their hand. [[Book money]] in a current account, by contrast, is a claim on a private commercial bank. The bank promises to exchange it for cash on demand or to execute it as a bank transfer.

The proportions are clear. In July 2026, currency in circulation in the euro area stood at €1,613 billion and the money supply M3 at €17,614 billion. Around 84% of what is colloquially regarded as money consists of bank deposits and is thus a liability of private banks. The two circuits touch at two points: at the cash machine and in payments between two banks.

bloecke.titel: A €300,000 property loan on two levels
bloecke.unter: At the top, central bank money flows between the banks, and at the same time book money flows between the customers at the bottom; these are two different kinds of euro.

bloecke.md:
The new deposit does not stay in the buyer's account. She transfers the €300,000 to the seller, who has his account at Bank B. Bank A has to settle this payment in central bank money, because Bank B does not accept book money from another bank.

Bank A therefore needs €300,000 in reserves. It borrows them on the money market from other banks or from the Eurosystem at the main refinancing rate, which has been 2.65% since 16 September 2026. As long as the deposit remained with Bank A, the bank also had to hold 1% of it as [[minimum reserves]]. That was €3,000, which has been remunerated at 0% since 20 September 2023.

At a refinancing rate of 2.65%, the minimum reserve therefore costs around €80 over a year, because the €3,000 itself earns no interest. Refinancing the €300,000 causes interest expense of around €7,950 a year. Lending is thus limited by the price of reserves and not by their quantity.

## The monetary aggregates M1, M2, M3

The ECB's monetary aggregates are graded by liquidity and build on one another. The further out a component lies, the harder it is to spend the amount immediately. The monetary base, often called “M0”, is not the innermost layer of M1, however. It is a quantity from the other circuit and consists of cash and the banks' balances at the central bank. Customers' sight deposits do not appear in it, and the banks' reserves are not included in M3.

bloecke.md:
In the familiar account, the central bank issues €100 of reserves. The bank keeps 1% and lends out €99, the next bank keeps 1% of the inflow and lends the rest on again, until a multiple of the original amount has been created. The minimum reserve ratio thus becomes an instrument with which the central bank controls the money supply.

The Bundesbank describes the [[money multiplier]] as a *reduced form*, that is, as the result of the interplay between banks, non-banks and the central bank and not as its cause. Excess reserves do not force any bank to grant a loan for which there is no solvent borrower. In addition, the direction of causality is the other way round. The loan comes first, and then the bank obtains the reserves it needs for it.

bloecke.titel: US money supply M2 divided by the monetary base
bloecke.unter: With a constant multiplier, the line would be horizontal. It fell from 9.2 to below 5 within months, because the Fed multiplied reserves without M2 growing accordingly.

bloecke.md:
## Limits to money creation

Reserves therefore do not limit money creation. Instead, four constraints act at the same time:

- The central bank sets the price by fixing the interest rate at which banks refinance themselves. If this rate rises, some lending projects become unprofitable, for the bank as well as for the borrower. The interest rate is therefore the instrument with which a central bank can steer lending.
- Regulation, through capital and liquidity requirements, ties every additional loan to scarce equity. A bank therefore cannot expand its balance sheet at will without breaching the ratios.
- Demand limits lending, because every loan needs someone who wants it and can service it. In July 2026, loans to the private sector in the euro area grew by 4.1% year on year, loans to households by 3.1% and loans to companies by 4.4%. M3 grew by 3.4% in the same month. Credit growth and money growth move largely in parallel, because one creates the other.
- The behaviour of non-banks also plays a role. If a customer moves a sight deposit into a ten-year bank bond, the money no longer counts towards M3, even though it has not left the bank. The measured money supply therefore also depends on the form in which households and companies want to hold their wealth.

The Eurosystem's balance sheet grew from around €1,154 billion at the start of 2007 to €8,836 billion on 24 June 2022. As a result of the run-off, it had shrunk to €5,911 billion by 11 September 2026. An almost eightfold increase was thus followed by a decline of a third, yet the money supply M3 did not follow these swings.

This is due to the two-tier structure of the monetary system. If the central bank buys a security from a bank, only central bank money is created, because the bank swaps a bond for a reserve balance. Nothing changes in M3. If, on the other hand, it buys from an insurer or a fund, book money is created as well, because the seller's bank credits the seller's account. Only this second part has a direct effect on the money supply.

Reserves do not circulate in the real economy. They cannot be transferred to a current account, and a company cannot buy anything with them. It is therefore inaccurate to equate bond purchases with printing money, as often happens. This equation ignores the boundary between the two circuits that this lesson is about.

A loan creates a deposit, and its repayment destroys it again. The money supply is therefore continuously determined as the balance of lending and repayment. It is not a fixed stock issued by any single body.

## The phrase “out of nothing”

In accounting terms the phrase is correct, because the €300,000 did not exist before the entry. It becomes misleading if it is taken to mean that the money is a gift. The new money is matched by a debt of the same size, with interest, a repayment schedule and default risk. The bank earns the difference between the interest it charges and the interest it pays itself. If the loan defaults, it loses equity. It therefore does not become richer merely by expanding its balance sheet.

This has two practical consequences. First, the money supply follows the credit cycle. If demand for credit collapses, the money supply shrinks without any authority having decided anything. This process is the central feature of every balance sheet recession. Second, the balance in a current account is legally a claim on a private company and not central bank money held in safekeeping by the bank. In normal times this difference does not matter; in a banking crisis, on the other hand, it is what matters most.

mitnehmen: Most money is created by a book entry when a commercial bank grants a loan; the deposit follows from the loan and does not precede it.
Central bank money and book money form two separate circuits, and around 84% of M3 in the euro area consists of bank deposits, that is, claims on private banks and not on the central bank.
The money multiplier is neither constant nor a control instrument; in the USA the ratio of M2 to the monetary base fluctuated between 9.2 and 2.8.
Money creation is limited by the refinancing rate, capital rules, credit demand and the investment behaviour of non-banks, not by the minimum reserve of 1%.
Repaying loans destroys money, which is why the money supply shrinks by itself in a credit crisis.

begriffe.text: Balances in accounts at commercial banks, also called deposit money. Legally it is a claim on the bank, and it is created mainly through lending. Such balances make up around 84% of the money supply M3 in the euro area.

Cash and banks' balances at their central bank. Only banks and holders of cash have access to it; together, the two parts form the monetary base. Payments between banks are settled in central bank money.
Simultaneous growth of the assets and liabilities sides of a balance sheet. When a loan is granted, the claim and the deposit are created in one step, without any change in equity.

Required balances that banks must hold at the central bank. In the Eurosystem 1%, essentially on customer deposits and paper with a maturity of up to two years, remunerated at 0% since 20 September 2023. They stabilise the money market because they only have to be met on average over six to seven weeks, but they do not limit money creation.

Ratio of the money supply to the monetary base. The value is neither constant nor the expression of a causal relationship. It is a ratio that results from the behaviour of banks, non-banks and the central bank.
